title: the Atharva Veda's healing hymns
hook: a hand on a forehead comes before any thermometer. one healing hymn ends right there, at the healer's own hands

segments.voice: Yesterday opened the Atharva Veda's healing hymns: a Veda that turns toward fevers, aches, and the people sitting up with them. If you were sick, what would you want a healing hymn to say? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-two.

A hand on a forehead. It's a check that comes before any thermometer. Someone leans over a sick child and lays a palm there, and the hand is asking a question: hot, or not? But something else happens too. The child's shoulders drop a little. Somebody is here. The hand is part of the answer before anyone knows what the answer is. In the Atharva Veda there's a healing hymn that ends right at that spot. Not with an herb, not with a potion, but with the healer looking down at their own two hands and speaking to them. Today: the hands that heal.
screen: `A HAND ON A FOREHEAD.` → `HOT, OR NOT?` → `SOMEBODY IS HERE.`

segments.voice: The hymn sits in the Atharva Veda's fourth book. In its last verses the healer turns and speaks, not to the patient and not to a god, but to their own hands. In paraphrase: this hand of mine is blessed. This other hand is more blessed still. This one holds every remedy. This one's touch is kind. Notice the order. One hand, then the other, and the second is praised even more. It's almost playful, like someone flexing fingers before a job. Then the next verse widens it. With these two hands of ten branches, and with the tongue that goes before speech, with these two healing hands, we touch you. Ten branches: the fingers, pictured like a tree. And the tongue is right there beside the hands. In this hymn, healing isn't touch alone or words alone. It's a voice speaking while the hands rest on someone. The hymn doesn't tell us who the patient was, or what was wrong. It keeps its attention on the healer's side of the bed, and on one quality above the others: the touch has to be kind, and the hands have to heal. On an ordinary day, that's a lot of hands. Hands that cook dinner for someone who's tired. Hands that rub a back. Hands that hold a phone and type something gentle, or something sharp. The hymn treats the plain human hand as something worth blessing out loud.
screen: `THE HEALER SPEAKS TO THEIR OWN HANDS.` · `ONE HAND BLESSED, ONE MORE BLESSED.` · `TEN BRANCHES, AND A TONGUE.` · `A KIND TOUCH THAT BRINGS NO HARM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet your own hands. Rest them in your lap, palms up. Feel their weight. Feel any warmth in the palms, any tingling in the fingertips. Ten branches. Then, if you like, lay one hand lightly on your chest or your forehead, as kindly as you'd touch someone you love. Let the touch be gentle, with nothing to fix. If you pray, you can hold someone who is unwell in mind while your hands rest. The bell holds the time.
The Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Today, one that ends with the healer's hands: one blessed, one more blessed still, holding every remedy, with a kind touch. Today's word.
screen: `THE ATHARVA VEDA'S HEALING HYMNS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Today, before your hands do one ordinary job for someone, a plate, a door, a message, notice them for a second, and let the touch be kind. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: The Atharva Veda's healing hymns are kept in Vedic recitation learned from a teacher, and Hindu families and priests draw on Vedic verses for blessing and for those who are unwell.

fork.setup: you're the healer at the bedside, and the hymn is nearly over. what do you turn to?
options: your own two hands, and your voice
fork.reveal: the hymn ends at the hands: with two hands of ten branches and the tongue that goes before speech, with these two healing hands, we touch you.

original.note: Sanskrit: all-healing, holding every remedy. Atharva Veda 4.13.6 says it of a hand.

trapdoor: what you thought: healing hymns are spells about herbs and potions.
what it means: this one ends with the healer's own hands and voice, touching gently, for healing.
what a scholar hears: ayam me hasto bhagavan, ayam me bhagavattarah, 'this hand of mine is blessed, this one more blessed still,' with the hand called vishvabheshaja, all-healing.

sources.ref: Atharva Veda 4.13.6–7 (this hand blessed, this one more blessed, holding every remedy, kind of touch; two hands of ten branches and the tongue that goes before speech, with these two healing hands we touch you)

sources.quoted: ayam me hasto bhagavan, ayam me bhagavattarah

notes: Editor: 'hands that bring no harm' (a loose rendering of anāmayitnu) changed to 'healing hands' in the teach, fork, trapdoor and source, so the lesson no longer builds on a reading the verse doesn't clearly give.
Hymn location: AV (Shaunaka) 4.13.6–7 is given from memory; the hand verse also appears as Rig Veda 10.60.12 (left out of the script under the claims rule). Confirm book, hymn and verse numbers.

Paraphrase of 4.13.6 (ayaṃ me hasto bhagavān ayaṃ me bhagavattaraḥ / ayaṃ me viśvabheṣajo 'yaṃ śivābhimarśanaḥ) as 'blessed / more blessed still / holds every remedy / touch is kind'; bhagavān could also be 'fortunate'. Confirm.

Paraphrase of 4.13.7 (hastābhyāṃ daśaśākhābhyāṃ jihvā vācaḥ purogavī / anāmayitnubhyāṃ hastābhyāṃ tābhyāṃ tvābhi mṛśāmasi) as 'two hands of ten branches, the tongue that goes before speech, hands that bring no harm, we touch you'. anāmayitnu is usually rendered 'healing' or 'free from disease'; 'bring no harm' is a soft rendering. Confirm.
The Sanskrit in the trapdoor is a simplified transliteration from memory; confirm.
